Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How can I go about finding companies who support individuals who are currently learning how to code?
Answer: Companies expect employees to be able to contribute to their bottom line within a reasonable period of time. If you're “learning how to code,” they may not see a return on investment for two years or more. And frankly not everyone has what it takes, so they may never get a productive programmer from the hire. You're not looking for a company as much as a college. If you can find any job where you can contribute, and where the job will grant you educational stipends, that can help, but in general if you are still learning to code, no company will likely want to hire you to code.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: I just started my bachelors in Computer Science. I want to be a software developer. What are the things that I should start doing right away to strengthen my career?
Answer: There are a number of good answers to this question, especially those that focus on building things. Write as much code as possible before you graduate. This is really the key, more than anything else. I'd like to add one twist: Really learn how to program rather than copying and pasting code or leaning on AI to fill in the details. It may not seem like much of a difference, but it really trains your brain to understand everything at a much deeper level. It may or may not make you a “10x” developer, but I can guarantee that any actual “10x” developers can write code from scratch without needing to copy and paste.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is it hard to build a good app if you don't have a good idea or money to hire a developer?
Answer: Is it hard? You don’t have a good idea, which means what? You have no idea what to build? You don’t have money to hire a developer, either? And presumably you don’t have the skill to build an app yourself? And you’re asking is it hard?! Sounds pretty well impossible to me given those constraints. You want to build an app yourself, but don’t know how to program? Look for no-code and low-code solutions and learn one. Play around with it until you’ve build several “apps” (they’ll be pretty trivial) and have a sense of what you can do with the no-code/low-code solution you choose. Then brainstorm for an idea that you can accomplish using those tools. Then at least you have a chance of getting the good idea you’ll need at a minimum to build a good app.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Does it make it too difficult for devs if I decide that I will create my own software and programs myself, then get a few professional developers to bug check and make sure my code is working efficiently before others can begin using it?
Answer: It… Depends? I can imagine a project simple enough where your work would be useful enough that a professional developer could just clean it up. But it's a pretty narrow set of requirements that a non-expert wouldn't make a mess of. And a mess is not something that a professional will want to clean up rather than rewrite it from scratch. For the simple reason that “fixing” the code you write will take more time and effort than just creating completely clean, well-designed code to begin with. So how can you tell the difference between a project you can meaningfully contribute to and one you can't? You pretty much need to ask an expert. 🤷🏻‍♂️

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Which is preferred and who will you hire: a team of collaborative, high-morale, and intuitively managed normal developers, or a team of arrogant rockstar x10 engineers facing morale, confusion, and management challenges?
Answer: I second the answer by Christopher F Clark. The entire meme of “arrogant rockstar 10x engineer” is a gross exaggeration at best, and a complete lie at worst. It's true that the very best engineers are more of a challenge to manage. But the very best engineers don't actually require much management, if any, and most of the “problems” reported by managers are the engineers objecting to stupid directions and rules. But morale problems? Really strong developers usually work well with each other. If there's a toxic developer or two in the group, then ditch them and your (slightly smaller) rockstar team will still likely outperform your team of normal developers. But why hire only one team? There are problems in most projects that can really benefit from a 10x developer, and there are more routine tasks that a 10x developer is kind of wasted on. The advantage of a strong developer is that they can solve the hard problems faster; on more routine tasks, they're probably not any faster at all. The book “The Mythical Man Month” is often credited as having popularized the idea of the 10x developer. But people seem to not know the entire story, which is that the book recommends a single strong developer per team as the team's “surgeon,” guiding the entire team, with supporting developers to handle the tasks that don't need a surgeon. So the right answer might be to break up the rockstars into several collaborating teams, spreading the “normal” developers around to each team. Not because the rockstars will have personality conflicts, but because the teams will be more efficient that way. All of this “rockstar” bashing gets old. Strong developers exist, and they can improve the entire trajectory of a project. Denying that they exist, or accusing them all of being arrogant assholes, says more about the bruised egos of the accusers than it says about actual 10x developers.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why are software engineer salaries relatively high in the USA compared to other countries?
Answer: I have a hypothesis on this. First, when you're looking at software jobs, you have to make the distinction between strong developers and average to mediocre developers. Back in the 70s, Fred Brooks wrote a book called the Mythical Man-Month, and among other things he pointed out that the best developers were between 5x-20x more effective than the least skilled. Today we talk about “10x” developers, referring to the same studies as Brooks, but I prefer to just say strong developers. So, the big, successful technology companies that are predominantly located in the US (the FAANG companies and Microsoft and others) have taken this extreme range of skill to heart, and they recognize that the abilities of strong developers reach beyond simply being faster; their code can be faster, more robust, and easier to reason about and modify. And more to the point, there are things a strong developer can achieve that a weaker developer will never successfully accomplish. Given the sheer number of technology companies in the US, and the relatively limited population of really strong developers, the salaries of those developers have been pushed up and up due to competition. A quick search finds estimates that Google alone employs at least 40,000 software engineers; if Amazon, Facebook, Apple, Netflix, and Microsoft each employ that many, we're talking nearly a quarter million software engineers being paid really high salaries. I believe that normal software engineers at the above companies make $200k+ total compensation at this point. Many make much more. FAANG companies have all effectively started to print money, and can justify the salaries since they're making more than a million dollars per software engineer in profits. This has been partly blamed on high cost of living areas requiring higher salaries, but that doesn't fully explain the difference. Picking a random comparison, salaries in San Francisco should be about 20% higher than those in London, according to one site.[1] Looking at the salary ranges, though, they're significantly more than 20% higher—and the Glassdoor numbers are low compared to the FAANG compensation I'm aware of. So you have a quarter million or more engineers who won't even talk to you unless you're offering $200k or more. Simply cornering that much of the market means that average companies have a smaller pool of developers to choose among. So there's a corollary effect where even average developers are making $75–150k. COVID probably amplified things even more. Many developers got a taste of working from home, and a lot of jobs are now 100% remote. I've had many FAANG recruiters contact me about remote positions in fact. So that removes some of the last vestiges of “high cost of living areas” being the cause of high salaries. Though obviously there was always a chicken-and-egg issue with that claim, since the extremely high cost of living wouldn't have been able to exist without high salaries to begin with. So in a nutshell, I think that's a large part of the issue. We may have a higher raw number of tech startups as well, considering the lax employment laws that make hiring less risky for the employer. That would be another increase in relative demand in software engineers, and a corresponding increase in salary due to the supply and demand curve. Higher overall demand, plus the recognition that the very best developers are worth large multiples of average developers, serve to inflate the salaries of all of the developers. This is fundamentally an only slightly educated guess. There may be other factors at play that I am completely clueless about. I have seen the vast gap between developer skill and developer compensation, which is loosely correlated, but beyond that—I'm a software engineer, not an economist, so your mileage may vary etc.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is doing software engineering in 2024 worth it? My term will end in 2029. Will there still be a demand of software engineers?
Answer: For the first question: Yes. But also, no. (If you feel the need to ask the question, odds are good the answer is no.) For the second question: Skilled and talented software engineers will be in demand for the foreseeable future. Full stop. Odds are good the demand will only increase relative to the supply over the next century. Here's the catch: Getting a degree doesn't make you skilled and talented. Spend some time trying to learn to program. Serious time: A year of regular effort should be enough. By the end of that year you should be able to tell whether software development is fun and interesting or if it seems like torture. Hint: If it seems like torture, you're not one of the skilled and talented. Related life hack: Don't pick the career that feels like torture. I'm not naive enough to suggest that everyone should love their job so much that they'd do it for free. That's a fantasy. But if you pick something you absolutely hate, you're setting yourself up for a life of misery—and don't expect particular success in your career, since you won't have the free energy to do what it takes to go the extra mile. If I were given a nickel for every time I saw someone complaining about how hard it was to keep up with current tech in programming…well, I'd probably be able to buy myself a dinner at an inexpensive restaurant. But talented developers who are successful don't complain about needing to learn. They generally like learning, so it's not a huge imposition to need to learn new ideas. The right aptitude makes it easy, in fact. Only you can answer the question as to whether you have that aptitude, though, and it might take a lot of work to figure it out. If you're asking the question, though, that's not a good sign. It indicates you might not really want to be studying software engineering, which implies that you really don't like the topic. If you're really just worried about whether it will continue to be a good career, then that's fine; it will, and frankly will probably be a good career for much longer than literally any other high paying job. By the time AI is ready to replace all software engineers, every single other career will already be able to be replaced by AI as well. Even careers requiring physical interactions like doctor, dentist, or surgeon.

Question: Is PHP still a goto language for web programming?
Answer: No. Pretty much not at all. WordPress is a go-to for low skill web developers to create cheap sites for clients. They will use PHP to customize the sites. So it's still used in a tremendous number of sites (with questionable security and typically awful performance). Even new sites. But it's not because PHP is a go-to language. It's because WordPress is the de facto cheap approach to creating sites. Are there developers who use PHP for things like Laravel? Sure. But they're in a pretty small minority compared to those who use Node, Java, C#, Python, Go, and even Ruby to create their sites. So in no way is PHP a go-to for anyone except those who have never bothered to transition to a better ecosystem. And all the ones I listed have better ecosystems today. Edit to add: No more PHP apologists please. Read the existing comments to this and my other answers if you want to see that a) I'm not just spouting outdated beliefs, and b) whatever your arguments are, I've already addressed them. Violators will have their comments deleted and will be blocked with prejudice. If you like PHP, by all means, use it and write your own answer about how great it is. Don't argue with me to try to convince me it doesn't suck, because I've heard all the arguments and they all fall flat when faced with the reality, which is that you're defending PHP because it's what you know, not because it's better. Of the dozens of people who have tried to come up with any reason it's better, exactly zero have succeeded. Zero. Any reasons you think you have are weak justifications for not spending the time to learn another ecosystem, and I'm sick of needing to address them again and again. Better to ask yourself why you feel so strongly that you need to defend the language? Is it because you're insecure about your beliefs? Edit2: Hateful trolls, or one with several sockpuppet accounts, have ruined it for everyone. Comments closed. This is why we can't have good things. Funny how emotional and ad hominem the attacks get. This is a programming language. For computers. The desperation in these comments pretty much prove what I said above: That the apologists are driven by insecurities. If I saw someone slamming a language I liked, I might make an attempt to correct their blatant errors or add a counterpoint if no one else had, but if there's already a wall of such, I'd downvote and move on. I certainly wouldn't stop to post insults about the author. Because that would undermine any point I thought I was making.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is it faster on average to have a balanced tree of if() else statements or to run through a bunch of if() else if() else statements?
Answer: This is part of what you learn when you earn a computer science degree. But you can also figure it out simply by counting. A string of, say, 16 if statements in series will take up to sixteen comparisons. If the statements require heavy calculations, then it could be 16x that you need to make that calculation. But if you instead can turn it into a perfectly balanced tree built only from if/else statements (meaning no if/else if situations), you can select among 16 results by using only four comparisons. Four is less than sixteen, so it would be faster. Whether that would matter in a real world program is another question. And if it does matter, it might not even be the fastest option. If you're checking if the same value equals one of a series of constants, a switch statement can sometimes be faster. Depends on the language and the exact situation, but in some cases the compiler can take it from four comparisons down to one. And a switch is easier to read. Sometimes what you really want is a table that maps states to behaviors. The speed wouldn't be any better than the perfectly balanced tree in some cases, but the clarity of the code would be vastly improved. Speaking of clarity of code, with too many branches of an if tree, you're probably doing something wrong from the point of view of design. Instead of calculating what should be done every time, for instance, you could use the strategy pattern[1] to assign an action to each object as appropriate. If you're looking at a series of thresholds to determine which gap a value is in, you should probably be traversing an array of the thresholds. Other patterns are available for other requirements. It's rare that you'd want to see 16 cases handled by as many if statements, no matter how your structure them.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Which one to use for web development: Python or Go?
Answer: Neither? There exist reasons to use Go. It's better than Python for most uses. Go’s static types are better than Python's type hints. Go is much faster. Go has a generally cleaner library. But if you're talking general web development, there's little motivation to use either. Probably the best of the popular approaches today is to use TypeScript and Node.js. Then your backend (which is all you can really create with Python and Go) can be written in the same language as, and share type declarations with, your frontend. Performance is good enough for most purposes. Support libraries are available for just about anything you can need. And the community is large. It's arguable that Blazor and C# is a better approach in some ways. I prefer the flexibility of TypeScript to the strictness of C#, as well as the breadth of the Node.js ecosystem, but for some web development of might be arguable that Blazor would be better. Flexibility can get you in trouble if you're not careful. The world is much larger than just Python and Go. Learn about more languages before making your decision.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is there a time when you join a software company and feel that the codes are too hard, the product too complicated, the framework and libraries too huge, and overwhelmed by the thoughts that you would never master them all? How would you overcome the fear, and train for the work? How long did it take you to master the code and make significant contributions to the project?
Answer: Hmmm… That's several questions. Note I'm a very senior developer, not a junior, so consider this an answer from experience. Do I ever find the code “too hard”? No. During my interview for any project I determine what expertise is required before I start, and no one so far has lied about what the requirements were. Do I find the product too complicated? Sometimes I find the architecture to be too complicated. Design is hard, and under development pressure, teams sometimes allow the architecture to grow organically. This kind of organic is not a good thing. Am I overwhelmed? Not really. On one project, the architecture was so bad that it took 20x longer than it would normally take me to accomplish anything, and that was stressful, but I always was confident that I could finish each task. Even on that last task I didn't fear it, nor did I “train” for it really. I asked questions and explored the different parts of the architecture to figure out how to accomplish the tasks they handed me. The other team members were only rarely available to answer questions, which was annoying, but I figured out ways to move forward. I made mistakes due to lack of information, but I was able to correct them when they told me the problems. And I was making minor contributions in a few days, and major contributions in a couple of weeks. I get that you're probably a junior developer. Keep learning and have faith you'll find the answers you need. It's a slog, but it's worth it.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How can I get a full stack developer to give me a price for the project I need completed and not just ask me what my budget is and would it be appropriate to ask that we break it up into smaller parts so I can more easily afford it?
Answer: There may be several things going on here. The developer may be trying to find out if it's worth doing any work with you at all. If your budget is too low, they might simply not be willing to put any time into the project. If you're asking for a fixed bid, then that takes a lot of work to generate. Depending on the complexity of a project, I tend to charge US$5k–20k just to make a plan based on your requirements. In a sense, you're asking for the developer to do that much work for you for free as well as to (presumably) do even more work for free if it turns out that their estimate was low. The developer may in fact be of the opinion that it's impossible to estimate a project in advance, and they're just trying to get a general sense of whether they might be able to complete enough of the project to be useful before you run out of money. Developers who follow this school of thought only work by the hour or week, and will give you an approximate number of weeks of work to complete the core of your project—and if that's too close to your budget already, they will instead say that your budget is too low. (Or they will take your money anyway and stop working when you run out—there are entirely too many developers who are effectively scammers out there). Finally, they may be doing what you're probably worrying about: Planning to charge as much as your budget will bear. This is especially likely if the project is totally simple; if, for instance, it's a mostly static site for a business, or if it's a simple storefront. To distinguish between the earlier options and the last, I would recommend finding a friend who is a good developer and asking them whether your project is simple, or if it has some kind of complexity or an unknown that might make it harder. Good luck.

Question: Why are Android phones better to be used by developers/programmers than iOS phones?
Answer: You shouldn't ask why until you ask whether. I use Android phones. I'm a software developer. The two are pretty much unrelated except for when I'm developing software for Android. I know software developers who like Android, and others who like iPhone. None that I'm aware of use their phone when they're programming, unless they're using their phone…as a phone. Name: Tim Mensch
Question: What can I do to improve my logic in programming? Everyone keeps saying “code code code code”, but how can one code all the time when they can't even build a logic to tackle the issue easily?
Answer: There's a point when you're learning to program—a threshold that you cross—where on one side of the threshold everything is a blur, and even though you've been learning all of the syntax of some programming language, you have no idea how to put the pieces together to build things. Then you cross that threshold and suddenly it starts to all make sense. If you can cross the threshold. I think there is a lot of well meaning advice given on how to learn to program, but what it comes down to in reality is the fact that you need to do enough programming to get your brain to make the right connections. To cross the bridge from confusion to comprehension. The “Learn X The Hard Way” tutorials (based on Learn Python The Hard Way) model roughly how I learned to program. Or rather, learned to think like a programmer. They have you type in code and explain how it works. There are likely other approaches that are effective, but it's a kind of immersion approach like you'd use to learn a human language. But that's why people tell you to code code code. It takes exposure for your brain to cross that threshold. To gain that understanding. And the uncomfortable truth is that some people never manage to cross that bridge. That includes some people who work as professional programmers—the kind that only barely get along by Googling for code to modify, or by using ChatGPT to write code for them. I can't tell you whether you just haven't tried hard enough yet or if you'll never get there. It might take a full year of practice to have the right insights; if you've been trying much longer than that, you might want to consider a career pivot. Good luck.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why do software engineers tend to consistently underestimate how much work a given effort takes?
Answer: Actually… We don't. Speak for yourself. 😜 Over the course of a huge project, though? What often happens is that some small number of tasks will take much longer than expected. Either you'll come across a previously unidentified requirement, or maybe something that you thought would be easy turns out to be much harder. Maybe an API doesn't work the way you expect. Or the code that works great on one system fails on others, requiring much more work to get it running smoothly everywhere. This is true for all engineering projects, by the way. I think I've seen a quoted average that construction projects tend to go over time and budget by something like 30%. And that's for projects that are generally well understood. In any event, when building something new, sometimes your assumptions are incorrect. So even if 98% of your estimates are spot on, that remaining 2% can take up 50% or more of the project time and cause extreme overruns.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is it extremely hard to be a good programmer? I am not sure how well structured and developed one’s brain should be, and I sense it is hard to be good at all aspects of programming.
Answer: Is it hard? It can be hard as you're initially learning. It can feel mysterious for quite a while. After a point, though, you either start to get good at writing code, and everything gets easier, or you have to keep slogging through memorization and look up how to do everything every single time, and that's your life until you burn out or transition to management. The first path is the one of a good programmer. The second is more of what I would call a scripter: A person who assembles code and tweaks it until it works, but who doesn't have the same depth of understanding of the software they write. The path of the good programmer isn't hard as much as challenging. The path of the scripter, from what I can see, is hard. Or rather it would be really hard for me if I had to work as long and jump through as many hoops to accomplish anything. In case it wasn't explicit, the difference isn't how hard you work, or how you learned, or who your mentor was. The difference is more in your aptitude, temperament, and curiosity. You can practice the curiosity, and you might be able to form a new temperament through force of will or force of habit. Those would likely be hard. But I'm not sure you have any control over the aptitude at all. The best advice I've come up with is to practice intentional learning. Stare at code until you can visualize its behavior. Then type in code that does what you need. Pretend you can't use copy and paste while you're learning. Run through dozens of practice problems, solving them without looking at example answers. Learn the art and craft of actually programming rather than the less elegant practice of duct taping of code together utilized by lower skill developers. If it didn't come easy to begin with, then it will likely be really hard to cross that bridge. But if you can make it, then the world of programming will open for you. And it will get easier. There will still be challenges, but with the right temperament, challenges can be fun. Is it really hard if you're enjoying the process?

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How would a software engineer advise someone who is looking to become a programmer and is hung up on learning the language that is the most popular in terms of job opportunities?
Answer: The thing you need to learn is how to think like a programmer. You can do that with any popular language. It doesn't really matter. It's much easier to learn your second language. Your first language may take a year or more of practice before you really start understanding what you're doing. Your second language shouldn't take more than a month. Your third language a week. If you don't believe me, then fine. Look at your local job listings. No answer on Quora will be able to tell you what is most common in your market, especially since you didn't tell us where you are. Look for job listings for JavaScript, TypeScript, Java, C#, and Python. Those are the best options for beginners that are also generally marketable. My key point, though, is that learning the syntax of the language isn't the hard part.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: In the software engineering profession, is it common to omit semicolons in JavaScript and rely on automatic semicolon insertion?
Answer: It's common, but in my opinion, it's ugly. It marks you as a JavaScript-only noob. JavaScript is a C-family language. One of the hallmarks of C-family languages is that they terminate every statement with a semicolon. JavaScript requires a semicolon at the end of every line. Omitting them and relying on ASI is like throwing trash on the street and relying on someone else to clean it up. Yes, someone will clean it up for you, but that doesn't make you any less of a slob. There are even cases where you can end up with code that doesn't behave the way you expect, and in the “standard” approach they have you add semicolons at the start of lines to fix the error (!!!). Considering the argument is that it makes things prettier, that seems a particularly poor resolution. Just use semicolons. It's not that hard, and if you use Prettier, it will add semicolons for you, so you don't even need to learn the habit of typing the character. Not that it's actually hard to type. I mean, C, Java, C#, and C++ developers have been adding semicolons for decades without their pinkies falling off, after all. It's a home row key! (At least on most Qwerty US English keyboards; YMMV). Everyone should be migrating to TypeScript as soon as they can anyway, and in TypeScript, the predominant standard is to use Prettier and require semicolons.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: As a software engineer, is it likely that employers will reject you if you quit your job to find a new job and you are unemployed while interviewing?
Answer: This is a prime example of answers that are really, “It Depends.” I have left jobs because I've gotten a better offer. I've left jobs when I wanted to do something new. I left one job over what comes down to office politics. The only time I've spent more than a few weeks looking for a job was right after 9/11 when no one was hiring because the country was in shock. I think I was looking maybe three or four months before something came up? But my resume looks good. It has from early in my career. I do well on programming challenges. I mostly do reasonably well in interviews (with some notable fails that aren't relevant to this discussion). So for me? I'd leave a job that was making me unhappy, because I'd be confident enough about finding another role that I wouldn't be stressed about it. But I keep hearing stories about developers who search for a new job for a year or more. Who have trouble with programming tests to the point of complaining about their use. Who freeze up in interviews. Who have resumes with very little to recommend them over all the other applicants. And if you've quit and are coming up on a hard deadline of “running out of rent money”? That's going to make everything to do with the interview even worse. So without even considering whether or not being unemployed makes them less likely to hire you, there are a lot of considerations that depend entirely on you. I have heard that, psychologically speaking, you seem more “attractive” as a hire if you're already in a job. But ultimately that only moves the needle a little. So in the situation where someone is otherwise right on the cusp, who maybe is up against someone else very similar, might get hired or not depending on whether they're currently employed. But my guess is that it's more likely that it wouldn't make any difference in most situations.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why are senior software engineering interviews so tough these days?
Answer: So, this is one of those questions that was asked years ago, and it has plenty of answers. But I think that I have a slightly different take on the situation. The industry is maturing, and more and more companies are demanding actual skill from their senior engineers. For a long time, because of the perpetual shortage of software engineers, standards were reduced, and developers with two years of experience who were barely doing more than copying and pasting code from Google were being hired in senior roles. But many of these companies have learned that simply having “senior” on their resume doesn't mean they can actually do the job. That if you do hire without extensive screening, you can end up with a developer who reduces the overall team velocity. Negative productivity is a thing. So for better or worse they've been adding various kinds of programming challenges to their interview process to try to avoid this problem. But then we get tons of formerly senior engineers who can't find a job posting questions about how hard it is to get through the interview process. This parallels the dichotomy between the “I always can pick up a new job quickly” crowd and the “no one is using reasonable criteria for hiring” crowd. The former have the skills required to be a senior software engineer in today's market, and the latter don't. Yes, jobs that don't require programming tests do still exist. By all means, they should keep applying for them and post self-righteous screeds about how they won't lower themselves to taking such tests, as if their real reason is some kind of high principle and not that they just can't write the code. But as the industry matures, more and more jobs will require actual skills. And people who write questions like this will find it harder and harder to get jobs, since they're competing with the many others who are lacking in programming competence. In summary: Senior software engineering interviews aren't tough at all if you have the right aptitude and experience. If you finding them to be tough, then you should try applying for a lower-than-senior role, or pivot to a role that's programming adjacent like QA or management. Because acting as if employers owe you a job even when you can't prove you can do it isn't a good look. If you want to comment on how unfair programming tests are, please take your complaints to this answer: Because I'm really sick of repeating myself. I've also already heard all of the arguments, and they all sound like “I can't write code and so therefore I'm going to claim that it's not relevant.” And considering the job is programming, being able to demonstrate that you can program at all seems like a reasonable test. If you're going to claim a programmer shouldn't need to have that skill, the proof is really on you.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: If you had to choose between an arrogant but brilliant programmer with weak collaboration abilities and an average programmer with strong cooperative skills, whom would you hire, and why?
Answer: There's no hesitation here. The brilliant programmer, hands down, no question. Brilliant software development is something that can't be taught. You either have or you don't. It's a rare enough aptitude that, when you find a developer who is genuinely good, you hire them. More than that, if you find a brilliant developer who is willing to work for you, you create a position for them so you can hire them now. Do not wait until you have a position available. Do not wait for the budget to be available. Hire them and figure out how the budget will work later. Make it happen. A brilliant developer can make the difference between barely getting a product done on time and finishing a product with enough time to spare while adding more features and fixing more bugs. About a developer having enough insight that they can anticipate and correct for potential problems. About being able to solve some problems that the average developer would never be able to overcome. So what if they don't have existing collaboration skills. You can teach people to collaborate. You can't teach them to be brilliant. Arrogance can be somewhat justified, but more to the point, brilliant developers are often accused of being arrogant when they're simply confident. But I'd put up with an arrogant, even abrasive, programmer, if they were willing to do what we asked. That said… I simply don't hire average developers. If I'm on a team, an average developer is likely not going to be good enough to keep up. So there really wasn't a choice from my point of view. Certainly, average developers do get hired, and from what I can tell, most of the places that hire average developers do select against brilliant developers. Larger companies especially have a hard time with developers who are several standard deviations above the mean, preferring to hire developers who are interchangeable instead of irreplaceable. So I'm really answering for only myself, and other answers that express preference for the personable developer aren't wrong. We just work at different kinds of companies.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: What is the future of programming and software engineering after AI? When will developers be completely replaced by AI?
Answer: Repeat after me: AI will replace all programmers sometime after every single other job has already been taken over by AI. Think of this the next time you watch a Roomba get stuck under a chair with an obvious exit and play its little “help, come rescue me!” song. Until you're engaging in intelligent conversations with AI friends who really seem to understand you, getting your therapy from AI therapists, being driven everywhere by AIs because that's how everyone gets around, and having your house cleaned and organized by AI assistants who quickly learn what items to put away and what you want to be left out, and who remind you of only the important things on your schedule that you need to prepare for, you don't need to start worrying about AI taking your programming job. Really. Parlor tricks like AutoComplete for blocks of code doesn't even really come close. It's cool, don't get me wrong, but it doesn't even scratch on the hard part of software engineering. It just means that software engineers won't need to type as much.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Are interviews harder than the job itself in software engineering?
Answer: I say no, with a helping of probably not. There's a myth that floats around that interviews are really hard, and that they require the candidate to solve these crazy hard problems, only to have their developers duct taping code together, never using the skills they needed to get the job. There are probably jobs out there that fit that description. I mean, it's a big world, after all. But most jobs today do benefit if you have the right skills to be able to solve a few relatively simple problems in about a half hour each. I think that most of the myth comes from the fact that people are actively training, even memorizing, common interview problems. It's fine to practice on Leetcode, don't get me wrong. Especially if you're using the time to learn new ways to think about algorithms! But memorizing fifty algorithms and interviewing dozens of times until you get an interview that happens to use the solution that you remember? That's cracking the interview in the sense of cheating to win, deceiving the interviewer about your skill because you happened to have memorized the question they used. It's worse when you look up what problems specific companies usually use; that's just straight up cheating. And once that programmer is hired, assuming they haven't been caught, they will quickly find the job is either completely beyond them, or they'll be delegated to simpler tasks (or in some cases unintentionally litter the code with small disasters). So in that respect, the interview may have been harder than the job. But it wasn't harder than the job they wanted the applicant to be able to do. They just decided to keep the programmer rather than firing them because firing someone is hard. Listen. The programming test exists to see if the candidate can create a novel bit of code. It shouldn't exist to see if the candidate memorized something. The current trend of studying hundreds of algorithms with the intent to memorize as many as possible simply perverts the whole process, because a regurgitated answer is a false positive in the interview. And I get that someone who studied CS really wants to get a job in software, and so they're motivated to do whatever it takes. But it sucks to be interviewing people who have turned our one measure of actual programming skill into a game they're trying to hack to give incorrect results in their favor. So if you're good at software engineering? The interview, including the programming test, should be easy compared to the job. And if you spend hundreds of hours trying to hack the interview process in your favor, the job may still be harder for you, unless you find that one company that gives hard problems but has really low actual job requirements.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Do rockstar software engineers dig deep and understand the implementation of programming languages and libraries that they use?
Answer: Controversial labeling aside*, the strongest engineers, in my experience, do understand at least how languages and libraries could be implemented. And often they understand the performance and memory characteristics guaranteed by the language or library as well. The phrasing “dig deep” isn't exactly how it works though. Forming a solid understanding of the fundamentals means that you can build up a mental model of how things probably work simply from the API. So it's not as if you need to spend hours reading source code of every library and programming language that you use, but instead just learning how something is intended to be used grants a mental model of how it likely works. Only when there is ambiguity do you need to dig deeper. And sometimes that digging is nothing more than checking the documentation. C++ standard library containers, for instance, let you know the expected performance and memory characteristics of each of the container options, so if you need to know the effect of a particular operation, you can look it up. That said, it's not too rare for a strong engineer to dig more deeply into a library when confronted by unusual behavior. I've submitted patches to many different open source projects either to fix bugs or to add features that I needed. One thing common to strong engineers is that we write our own code instead of relying on example code, so we're more likely to do things in ways that haven't been fully tested by the community. That means we often find obscure bugs where libraries don't work as expected. But in the general case, no, we don't dig into every tool we use. I've been using a lot of TypeScript on Node.js, for instance, but haven't tried to understand exactly how the JIT compilation of V8 works. I have read about how it works at a high level, but that was mostly out of curiosity rather than for concrete benefits. And that's the final piece of the puzzle, in my opinion. In addition to a strong grasp of the fundamentals, a strong engineer needs curiosity. You don't get to the point where you're strong if you don't have the drive to learn what you don't know about how something works. * Hardly anyone uses “rockstar” in a non-ironic manner any more. The label 10x is far more common. The other answers, as I write this, are all making fun of the term “rockstar” rather than making any attempt to answer, though at least one doesn't seem to believe that strong developers even exist, as if software engineering is the sole human endeavor where all humans are magically exactly equal in skill, unlike every other skilled endeavor from writing books to art to advanced mathematics.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How are software engineers and full-stack web developers different? I asked this question because I wanna do just something (solving problems, creating new features, and thinking about it) Without any domain specifics. How should I do?
Answer: It sounds like you're asking for some kind of “pure software engineering” in the same vein as “pure mathematics.” Such a thing might exist in academia, but at that point you're doing computer science research, not software engineering. Software engineers, kind of by definition, are building something. That's what engineers do. And you can't find people to pay you software engineer wages to build software that completely lacks a domain. In some cases the domain may be a software domain. Database development is itself a domain, for instance. Working on a web site that manages a to-do list might not require any industry domain knowledge, but it does require you to learn web or backend development and all of the relevant libraries and frameworks that you need to deal with. And even then you may need to understand user privacy laws like the GDPR. If you're just saying that you don't want to learn a million arbitrary rules to work on banking or PCI compliance software, or the huge set of rules surrounding medical compliance, or any other heavily regulated industry? Then in that case just learning engineering and picking up details on the job is all you'll likely need. But there is no getting around at least some form of domain learning if you want to work in software. As to your specific question: There's no generally agreed upon definition for software engineer or full stack developer. In my own definition, a software engineer uses software engineering principles and has a deep understanding of what it is they're building, whether it be a web site, server backend, mobile app, or firmware for an IoT device. Whereas a full stack developer can create a frontend and backend for a web site, and probably knows HTML, JavaScript/TypeScript plus maybe an additional server language, and how to interact with at least one database, but may or may not be a software engineer by my definition. Hint: A software engineer doesn't need to copy and paste code or use AI to generate code. I use AI all the time at this point, but it's generally as a semantic search of the docs. Aside from the template to start a new app, though, or the very occasional (like, once a week or less) block of code to do something obscure, it's literally multiple times faster for me to write the code to get the result I want than to try to convince an AI to produce that code. That doesn't mean I won't use autocomplete when it pops up, if it saves me some time and produces what I was going to type anyway. But the point is I could have typed the code. You can't engineer something if you don't understand the pieces you're using, and if you can't build something from scratch with those pieces, you don't really understand them. And when you understand software development at a deep level, you can pick up the domain knowledge you need as you need it. So endeavor to become a software engineer. The rest should follow.

Question: How do web programmers divide the running part of code between the server-side and the client-side more efficiently nowadays? Is it always better to run more code on the server-side if too many requests are coming?
Answer: That's two very different questions. Second part first: That's pretty much exactly wrong. If you want to scale more easily, then you want to run as little code on the server as possible. As to how to “divide” the code? That's a matter of design, and the accumulated wisdom developers gain that grants them the intuition to ensure the right code is in the right place. You need to understand the goals of the system you're creating. And that includes the security requirements. When you understand what you need to create, how to “divide” the code becomes obvious. And until you understand what you need to create, no pithy advice that can be offered on Quora will help.

Question: I don’t know what to do anymore. I don’t want a future and I’m 14. I just want to be in a grave atp. I’ve asked for help over and over. I’ve tried hotlines. What do I do?
Answer: It can really suck to be 14. I had problems with depression at that age. I hated school. I was in conflict with my parents. I wanted attention, but when I got attention it was negative and it made things worse. Know that life gets better. It won't be like this forever. My life is awesome now, and I wouldn't want to have missed out on it for anything. Do what you can to put up with it. If there's something that you like, that you really resonate with, dive into it (as long as it's safe!) and let it distract you as much as possible until you finish high school. I'm thinking music, videos, hobbies, books, anime, clothing, makeup, animals, technology—whatever you can lose yourself in. And I know that high school seems like forever, but it really isn't. If you put your mind to it, you'll endure. You're stronger than you think. You haven't said if there are specific people bothering you, but there's a great quote floating around that goes something like: Revenge is outliving your enemies. If you can learn to live well, so much the better. If there are school counselors, talk to one. If you get desperate and nothing I've said works, then let a counselor know that you're having these thoughts, and they should get you the help you need. If the first counselor doesn't help you, then find another, or try the hotlines again, or as a last resort dial 911. That's better than making any decision that would be final. If you make it through, your life will change, and it will likely be for the better. You're in a period of transition right now, and that can really suck, but if you can hold on just a little longer, there's a better life waiting for you.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: As a software engineering manager what would you do when a highly skillful software engineer in your team habitually deletes code developed by other developers and writes their own implementation which is much more superior?
Answer: This is a skilled developer who is otherwise getting their assigned work done and working as a team player? And the changes are really improvements and not just minor aesthetic changes? Then I’d encourage them to work on communication skills, and possibly encourage individual team members to not feel as proprietary about their code. Beyond that, poor question grammar aside, it sounds like you’re asserting that the replacement implementation is superior to the code that’s been replaced. Unlike other takes on this, I’m going to say that if a developer is reducing overall technical debt on a project without impacting their ability to get their assigned work done, that’s a good thing. But at the same time, since this question comes up at all, there must be some kind of conflict. What comes to mind is that other team members are feeling offended by this developer’s actions. So where are the communication issues I mentioned? The developer should take many of these changes as opportunities to teach other team members better ways to approach problems. Just changing code every time they see it isn’t the “correct” structure actually makes more work for them, and ideally they should be motivated to teach their techniques to other team members. Now I wouldn’t demand heroic attempts to teach the rest of the team; some programmers are less amenable to learning from coworkers, and if they aren’t interested in learning, that’s their issue. As to the likely motivation for this question: You aren’t your code. Developers need to realize that, once their code has been released to the team that others may come in and change it. If you’re going to be on a team with a skilled developer and you don’t want to hamstring that developer, then you need to put on your big-boy or big-girl pants and accept that sometimes your code will be improved when this developer happens to make changes in its vicinity. Now if the developer is spending half of the week going through and rewriting every line of code released by the remainder of the team? Or if the extra rewriting is causing their own responsibilities to slip? That’s a problem. And if the project doesn’t have sufficient test coverage that you can be confident that any changes made by the skilled developers are producing substantially the same (or better) results? That’s a different problem. But if the project has sufficient coverage that rewrites of blocks of code are known to produce valid results when they’re complete, and the developer is able to quickly rewrite the blocks of code required to work on the tasks they’re working on anyway? I see absolutely no reason to ask them to stop, and anyone who has a knee-jerk response to tell them to stay in their lane should not be surprised when all of their skilled developers leave the team for greener pastures.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is a software engineer constantly judged by the quality of code that they produce?
Answer: It depends a lot on the company. Some companies get it right, which means, in part, raising the overall code quality over time. This means code review, and what is code review but judgement of the quality of code? Some (many? Most?) companies really don't get it right. There are managers who aren't code savvy directing programmers, and there are no processes in place to review code before it's integrated. A developer will still be judged for poor code, but not constantly. Instead the judgement will be reserved for when their code causes problems that come to the attention of management, or that other developers are assigned to fix. When one team member who contributes for three months and then leaves the project turns out to be responsible for 80% of the bugs needing to be fixed over the next eight months (true story), then is that programmer going to be judged? I don't see how we could avoid feeling that judgment without being saints. And then there are the users of the product. If I'm using, say, the Quora app, and it operates in some unreasonable manner or has really annoying bugs that haven't been fixed in years, will I judge the programmers harshly? Yes, I will. I know there is time pressure and deadlines and so forth, but many of the problems shouldn't have existed to begin with, so yes, I judge those programmers. But are they being judged by their employer? Who knows. Maybe they are being praised for meeting deadlines and achieving goals. Not all companies actually care about quality, after all. So I guess if you're wary of being judged by your employer, you should try to join companies with crap software. Odds are good your code won't be judged by anyone who pays you, though the users might post passive-aggressive insults on the very product you're creating. Just saying.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How do programmers deal with their job when they are old? I am always thinking about how I am going to deal with my job when I may not be too productive. Can I still learn new things? Will it still be possible to sit 14 hours in front of the monitor?
Answer: I think the young underestimate the old. I have zero trouble learning new technologies and frameworks and even languages, and I'm old. But I don't spend 14 hours in front of a monitor…almost ever. It may happen if I'm really engaged in a project. But it always results in my taking time off shortly thereafter. That said, I didn't spend often 14 hours in front of my computer when I was younger either, again unless I was really engaged. I wrote a lot of video games when I was younger, so I was really engaged in what I was doing more often. And there have been occasional crunch times on projects. That seems inevitable. But…14 hours? Nine, or maybe ten hours of actual work with a couple of breaks is more like it. Past that and your productivity drops to the point where it's effectively zero or negative, at least over the long haul. I'd say that if your job makes you work 14 hours per day that you need to find another job. No one should be asked to work that much, and I can't believe that your employer is producing reliable software if they treat their developers like that. The only employers that treat developers like that are sweat shops that crank out code that's just good enough to fool their clients (marks) into continuing to pay them. You're taking part in a scam, in other words. Or if you're the only one who works that long to keep up, or if the reason that you aren't looking for another job is that you can't pass the interview process for a more ethical employer? Then you should probably be looking for another career now. No need to wait until you're older. Some people aren't cut out to be software developers. Better to decide that early and pivot to another career.

Question: Is the Coding Ninjas certificate valuable?

Question: Why don't companies build neighborhoods of smaller more affordable ($80-150k) homes?
Answer: The cost to build an expensive house is higher than building a “cheap” house, but the profit margin for the expensive house goes up much more quickly. So if you're a developer and own some amount of land, expensive homes will make you much more money per square foot of land than cheap homes. There is a name for actual cheaper housing that you can find: Condos. When you don't need to build as many exterior walls, there is appreciably less work, and less work means less expense. If you want places to live that are even cheaper, then you need the government to step in, either by requiring some units of every development to be price controlled, or by building some homes directly and renting or selling those units to residents. Again, though, you're probably going to get condos or at least townhouses if your want genuinely cheap housing. At least unless you're living in an area where it either snows in the winter or gets extremely hot in the summer. LA apparently is building tiny homes for the homeless, for instance. [1]

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is it okay for a software engineer to say that they don’t want to do a specific job (e.g., training doc, manual regression testing, etc.) when assigned by their manager?
Answer: So… Finding myself shocked at the number of “only if you want to be fired” answers. I mean, if I've been hired as a backend engineer, with the understanding that I'd be working on the new architecture, and instead they started assigning me to fixing frontend bugs, I'd absolutely push back. I can do the work, but I'm always clear in my negotiations what I want to be working on. So to all of the people who have been warning us that we'll be fired if we said no to a request, I have a simple response: Well before they got around to firing me, I'd have resigned my position if they kept insisting. I mean, I've almost never had trouble getting a new gig, and odds are good that I'd have one lined up well before the HR machine could have worked it's way through the mandatory PIP and warnings and so forth. In practice, though? I've refused manager requests that I didn't find to be reasonable many times. The consequence is… They ask again the next week. Using stronger language, sometimes. And I'd ignore the new requests in a loop until they gave up asking or I quit. A good software engineer has a golden ticket. They aren't completely proof against being let go, as recent FAANG layoffs demonstrate, but in general, if they're actually a good engineer, they have job security. If the reason they're asking you to do manual regression testing of writing documentation is that the team has requested that you stop writing code, though? Because the code you write causes them more work than if they'd written the code themselves from scratch? Then you're not a software engineer, title notwithstanding, and they're trying to be nice by giving you something productive to work on rather than just firing you. In that situation, it's agree with the other answers: If you're being asked to stop programming, then that means your days at the job are numbered if you don't comply—and odds are good you won't be able to easily walk into another job if your skills are weak. To me, it's about respect. You don't hire me as a programmer and then expect me to spend all of my time doing manual regression testing. Now should I test to see if the code I wrote broke something? Well, yes, duh, that's part of the programming job. You don't write code but then never test it! But if they're asking you to sit around testing instead of programming? Then you're not performing the duties of a software engineer.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is there a gap between how software engineers think compilers work and how they actually work?
Answer: All abstractions are leaky. If a developer has no clue at all how a compiler, or more to the point, the low level assembly code could work, then ignorance of the lower levels can cause just as many problems as not understanding how a framework, an ORM, or even how a service like AWS could work. You don't need to implement AWS to have some idea how it would be implemented, and therefore what the drawbacks or performance characteristics might be. You don't need to step through every line of source of the ORM you're using to understand what it must be doing with respect to its actual queries. You don't need to know the implementation details of your framework to know what the performance characteristics of your design decisions might be. You don't need to know exactly how the compiler you're using works either, but knowing that it's more expensive to compare strings than integers, knowing the dangers of comparing floats, and knowing and internalizing the kinds of computational complexity a compiler can and can't help you with is extremely useful in creating code that isn't unintentionally pessimized (the opposite of optimized). Treating any aspect of infrastructure or your tools as magical black boxes is a path to creating code disasters, because if you don't understand what you're doing, you're far more likely to make stupid mistakes.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes better at writing code than humans, will coding become less important in the future?
Answer: Premise false. In no way is AI better at writing code than humans. Nor is there any trajectory in that direction at the moment. Right now AI is only able to regurgitate code that was already written by humans. When being asked to accomplish very simple tasks, it can even regurgitate code that's correct. But it's atrociously bad at writing novel code, for the simple reason that no current technology embodies any understanding into the AI models. And since it periodically spits out code that's laughably bad, the code is only useful to a programmer who knows how to fix it or rewrite it. Programming isn't just specialized typing. It's not simply memorizing syntax and translating the English description of a project into code. It requires that the programmer understand the goal of the code they're writing. It requires the programmer be able to design the overall architecture of the application. AI can do none of this. Zero. Zilch. Null-pointer-exception, reference-not-found level of nothing when searching for any actual understanding in the current models. But that's all ignoring the elephant in the room: Coding is not, nor has it ever been, the hard part. Only beginners who are trying to avoid actually learning to code think it's hard. I suspect the same people who used to ask questions about programming “in plain English” are now hoping that AI will prevent them from needing to learn the syntax of a language. A bit later in the beginner's journey, they often end up asking “I've learned [Python/JavaScript/Ruby/Java/etc.] completely, but I still don't know how to make X. What am I doing wrong?” These beginners have had their first real insight into programming: Learning the syntax of a language doesn't magically make them a programmer. Conversely, once you do learn to think like a programmer, you can transition to another language quickly. Using AI can, in fact, speed up this process. But given that there are only on the order of a half dozen popular languages you might be required to use at any one time, and the AI will only cut a week or so off of the learning process, there's only about six weeks of potential time savings for any one developer—and that's mostly across their whole career, so not even six weeks per year. My point is that “learning to think like a programmer” is the hard part, and AI can't do that at all. Learning to code will be required as a part of programming for the foreseeable future, and it's actually the easier part of learning to program. If learning to code is so hard that you're desperate to figure out ways around doing the learning, I might recommend a career/major change to a domain that is more compatible with your brain. Programming isn't for everyone.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: 13 (f) who wants to be successful in life like business and has many dreams. Yet I’ve got poor motivation and I don’t know how to change that or what to do. I need someone to talk to that can change my mind-set to better. Any help or tips?
Answer: Try to get evaluated for ADHD. Talk to a school counselor. It presents differently for different people, and can vary even more for young women. And a lack of motivation is one of the main symptoms. Note that you can have ADHD and still do well in school if you're sufficiently anxious about getting your work done. This is why a lot of people with ADHD never get diagnosed. Also Google for ADHD coping strategies. Even if you can't get an official diagnosis, there are approaches you can learn that can help, if that's truly your issue. Good luck.
